questions.question: Is your system an AI system within the meaning of the AI Act?
questions.ownerContext: An AI system is usually software, or a component of software, that infers (derives) how to produce an output or course of action from patterns learned from data (machine learning) or by reasoning over logic (logic-based) or knowledge (knowledge-based), rather than merely following precise, pre-set instructions. It can operate with varying degrees of autonomy; it does not have to function entirely without human involvement. While not required, it can keep learning and change its behaviour while in use.​‌
questions.coContext:
AI Act Provisions

AI System means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments (EU AI Act. Art. 3 (1))

Recitals

Recital (12): The notion of ‘AI system’ in this Regulation (...) should be closely aligned with the work of international organisations working on AI (...). Moreover, the definition should be based on key characteristics of AI systems that distinguish it from simpler traditional software systems or programming approaches and should not cover systems that are based on the rules defined solely by natural persons to automatically execute operations. A key characteristic of AI systems is their capability to infer. This capability to infer refers to the process of obtaining the outputs, such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions, which can influence physical and virtual environments, and to a capability of AI systems to derive models or algorithms, or both, from inputs or data. The techniques that enable inference while building an AI system include machine learning approaches that learn from data how to achieve certain objectives, and logic- and knowledge-based approaches that infer from encoded knowledge or symbolic representation of the task to be solved. The capacity of an AI system to infer transcends basic data processing by enabling learning, reasoning or modelling. The term ‘machine-based’ refers to the fact that AI systems run on machines. The reference to explicit or implicit objectives underscores that AI systems can operate according to explicit defined objectives or to implicit objectives. The objectives of the AI system may be different from the intended purpose of the AI system in a specific context. For the purposes of this Regulation, environments should be understood to be the contexts in which the AI systems operate, whereas outputs generated by the AI system reflect different functions performed by AI systems and include predictions, content, recommendations or decisions. AI systems are designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, meaning that they have some degree of independence of actions from human involvement and of capabilities to operate without human intervention. The adaptiveness that an AI system could exhibit after deployment, refers to self-learning capabilities, allowing the system to change while in use. AI systems can be used on a stand-alone basis or as a component of a product, irrespective of whether the system is physically integrated into the product (embedded) or serves the functionality of the product without being integrated therein (non-embedded).

EC Guidelines on the definition of an artificial intelligence system (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-ai-system-definition-facilitate-first-ai-acts-rules-application):

(14) The second element of the definition refers to the system being ‘designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy’. Recital 12 of the AI Act clarifies that the terms ‘varying levels of autonomy’ mean that AI systems are designed to operate with ‘some degree of independence of actions from human involvement and of capabilities to operate without human intervention’.
 
(17) The reference to ‘some degree of independence of action’ in recital 12 AI Act excludes systems that are designed to operate solely with full manual human involvement and intervention. Human involvement and human intervention can be either direct, e.g. through manual controls, or indirect, e.g. though automated systems-based controls which allow humans to delegate or supervise system operations.
 
(22) The third element of the definition in Article 3(1) AI Act is that the system ‘may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment’. The concepts of autonomy and adaptiveness are two distinct but closely related concepts. They are often discussed together but they represent different dimensions of an AI system’s functionality. Recital 12 AI Act clarifies that ‘adaptiveness’ refers to self-learning capabilities, allowing the behaviour of the system to change while in use. The new behaviour of the adapted system may produce different results from the previous system for the same inputs.
 
(31) This clarification explicitly underlines that the concept of ‘inference’ should be understood in a broader sense as encompassing the ‘building phase’ of the AI system. Recital 12 AI Act then provides further guidance on techniques that enable this ability of an AI system to infer how to generate outputs. Accordingly, the techniques that may be used to enable inference include ‘machine learning approaches that learn from data how to achieve certain objectives and logic- and knowledge-based approaches that infer from encoded knowledge or symbolic representation of the task to be solved.’
 
(39) In addition to various machine learning approaches discussed above, the second category of techniques mentioned in recital 12 AI Act are ‘logic- and knowledge-based approaches that infer from encoded knowledge or symbolic representation of the task to be solved’. Instead of learning from data, these AI systems learn from knowledge including rules, facts and relationships encoded by human experts. Based on the human experts encoded knowledge, these systems can ‘reason’ via deductive or inductive engines or using operations such as sorting, searching, matching, chaining. By using logical inference to draw conclusions, such systems apply formal logic, predefined rules or ontologies to new situations. Logic- and knowledge-based approaches include for instance, knowledge representation, inductive (logic) programming, knowledge bases, inference and deductive engines, (symbolic) reasoning, expert systems and search and optimisation methods. For example, classical language processing models based on grammatical knowledge and logical semantics rely on the structure of language,
questions.examples:
- AI-enabled e-mail spam detection system: trained on e-mails that humans labelled "spam" or "not spam", it then classifies new e-mails on the basis of the patterns it has learned Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 33
- Image classification systems, medical diagnostic systems trained on labelled medical images, and fraud detection systems trained on labelled transaction data Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 34
- AI systems used in drug discovery that group chemical compounds and predict potential new treatments (unsupervised learning) Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 35
- Language models that learn to predict the next token in a sentence (self-supervised learning) Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 36
- AI-enabled robot arm that learns to grasp objects by trial and error (reinforcement learning) Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 37
- Early-generation expert systems for medical diagnosis, built by encoding the knowledge of medical experts and drawing conclusions from a patient's symptoms (logic- and knowledge-based approach) Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 39
- AI systems in self-driving cars, and AI systems that estimate energy consumption from smart-meter data, weather forecasts and consumer behaviour Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 55
- Autonomy: a system that needs manually provided inputs but generates its output by itself, and an expert system that on the basis of human input produces a recommendation on its own, both have "some degree of independence of action" Source: Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, C(2025) 5053 final, para 18

questions.question: Is the AI System or its output used exclusively for one or more of the following matters?
questions.ownerContext:
MILITARY, DEFENCE AND NATIONAL SECURITY
The AI Act does not cover an AI system that is used only for military, defence or national security purposes. It does not matter who uses it: a public body and a private company are treated alike. If the same system is also used for any other purpose, for example civilian, humanitarian or law enforcement, even occasionally, the exclusion is lost.

SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
The AI Act also does not cover AI systems that are developed and used only for scientific research and development. This includes research in all fields, not only technical sciences, but also the humanities and social sciences.

KEY CONDITION: "EXCLUSIVELY"
The key word is "exclusively". If the system is also used for any other purpose (for example civilian, commercial or law enforcement), the AI Act applies. The same is true if a system first built for military use is later used, even temporarily, for civilian or humanitarian purposes.

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
MILITARY, DEFENCE AND NATIONAL SECURITY (EXCEPTION IA)

Summary:
Art. 2(3) contains three separate rules: (1) areas outside the scope of Union law and the Member States' national security competences, (2) AI systems used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, (3) AI systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union whose output is used in the Union exclusively for those purposes. Recital 24 explains the rationale (Art. 4(2) TEU) and the consequences of mixed use or a later change of purpose. Look here for: the "exclusively" test, the wording "regardless of the type of entity", and what happens when a system is also used for civilian, law enforcement or public security purposes.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (3).  This Regulation does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law, and shall not, in any event, affect the competences of the Member States concerning national security, regardless of the type of entity entrusted by the Member States with carrying out tasks in relation to those competences.

This Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.

This Regulation does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union, where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.

Recitals:
Recital (24): If, and insofar as, AI systems are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification of such systems for military, defence or national security purposes, those should be excluded from the scope of this Regulation regardless of which type of entity is carrying out those activities, such as whether it is a public or private entity. As regards military and defence purposes, such exclusion is justified both by Article 4(2) TEU and by the specificities of the Member States’ and the common Union defence policy covered by Chapter 2 of Title V TEU that are subject to public international law, which is therefore the more appropriate legal framework for the regulation of AI systems in the context of the use of lethal force and other AI systems in the context of military and defence activities. As regards national security purposes, the exclusion is justified both by the fact that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States in accordance with Article 4(2) TEU and by the specific nature and operational needs of national security activities and specific national rules applicable to those activities. Nonetheless, if an AI system developed, placed on the market, put into service or used for military, defence or national security purposes is used outside those temporarily or permanently for other purposes, for example, civilian or humanitarian purposes, law enforcement or public security purposes, such a system would fall within the scope of this Regulation. In that case, the entity using the AI system for other than military, defence or national security purposes should ensure the compliance of the AI system with this Regulation, unless the system is already compliant with this Regulation. AI systems placed on the market or put into service for an excluded purpose, namely military, defence or national security, and one or more non-excluded purposes, such as civilian purposes or law enforcement, fall within the scope of this Regulation and providers of those systems should ensure compliance with this Regulation. In those cases, the fact that an AI system may fall within the scope of this Regulation should not affect the possibility of entities carrying out national security, defence and military activities, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities, to use AI systems for national security, military and defence purposes, the use of which is excluded from the scope of this Regulation. An AI system placed on the market for civilian or law enforcement purposes which is used with or without modification for military, defence or national security purposes should not fall within the scope of this Regulation, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.


SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT (EXCEPTION IB)

Summary:
Art. 2(6) excludes AI systems and models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Recital 25 explains the rationale and the limits of the exclusion (e.g. systems placed on the market as a result of research remain covered; other systems used for research remain subject to the Regulation). Recital 109 concerns general-purpose AI models and persons who develop or use models for non-professional or scientific research purposes. Look here for: the "sole purpose" wording and the ethical and Union-law conditions that apply to research and development.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (6). This Regulation does not apply to AI systems or AI models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.

Recitals:
Recital (25): This Regulation should support innovation, should respect freedom of science, and should not undermine research and development activity. It is therefore necessary to exclude from its scope AI systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Moreover, it is necessary to ensure that this Regulation does not otherwise affect scientific research and development activity on AI systems or models prior to being placed on the market or put into service. As regards product-oriented research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models, the provisions of this Regulation should also not apply prior to those systems and models being put into service or placed on the market. That exclusion is without prejudice to the obligation to comply with this Regulation where an AI system falling into the scope of this Regulation is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity and to the application of provisions on AI regulatory sandboxes and testing in real world conditions. Furthermore, without prejudice to the exclusion of AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, any other AI system that may be used for the conduct of any research and development activity should remain subject to the provisions of this Regulation. In any event, any research and development activity should be carried out in accordance with recognised ethical and professional standards for scientific research and should be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law.
questions.examples:
- [Not excluded] An AI system developed for military purposes that is used outside those purposes, temporarily or permanently, for law enforcement or public security purposes: it falls within the scope of the AI Act. Source: Recital (24) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not excluded] An AI system placed on the market or put into service for a military purpose and, at the same time, for a non-excluded purpose such as civilian purposes or law enforcement: it falls within the scope of the AI Act. Source: Recital (24) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Excluded] An AI system placed on the market for civilian or law enforcement purposes which is used, with or without modification, for military, defence or national security purposes. Source: Recital (24) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Excluded] An AI system specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not excluded] Any other AI system that is merely used for the conduct of research and development activity remains subject to the AI Act. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

allowedAnswers.label: Military, defense or national security purposes

questions.question: Is the AI System used by a public authority of a third country OR an international organisation for international cooperation or law enforcement?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not apply to public authorities of non-EU countries or to international organisations when they use AI systems as part of cooperation with the EU or with EU Member States in the fight against crime or in judicial matters.

CONDITIONS (ALL MUST BE MET)
All of the following conditions must be met:
- the user is a public authority of a non-EU country or an international organisation,
- the system is used under an international cooperation framework or agreement on law enforcement or judicial cooperation with the EU or with one or more Member States,
- the non-EU country or organisation provides adequate safeguards to protect people's fundamental rights and freedoms.

RESPONSIBILITY OF EU AND NATIONAL AUTHORITIES
EU and national authorities that use the results of such systems in the EU still remain responsible for complying with EU law.

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION - THIRD-COUNTRY AUTHORITIES AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATIONS

Summary:
Art. 2(4) sets out the exclusion for public authorities of third countries and international organisations using AI systems in the framework of international cooperation or agreements on law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or Member States, subject to adequate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms. Recital 22 explains the purpose (preventing circumvention of the Regulation while allowing cooperation with foreign partners), who should assess whether the safeguards are adequate, and that EU and national recipients of such outputs remain accountable for compliance with Union law. Look here for: the wording "adequate safeguards" and the role of the supervisory authorities.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (4) This Regulation applies neither to public authorities in a third country nor to international organisations falling within the scope of this Regulation pursuant to paragraph 1, where those authorities or organisations use AI systems in the framework of international cooperation or agreements for law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or with one or more Member States, provided that such a third country or international organisation provides adequate safeguards with respect to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals.

Recitals:
Recital  (22): In light of their digital nature, certain AI systems should fall within the scope of this Regulation even when they are not placed on the market, put into service, or used in the Union. This is the case, for example, where an operator established in the Union contracts certain services to an operator established in a third country in relation to an activity to be performed by an AI system that would qualify as high-risk. In those circumstances, the AI system used in a third country by the operator could process data lawfully collected in and transferred from the Union, and provide to the contracting operator in the Union the output of that AI system resulting from that processing, without that AI system being placed on the market, put into service or used in the Union. To prevent the circumvention of this Regulation and to ensure an effective protection of natural persons located in the Union, this Regulation should also apply to providers and deployers of AI systems that are established in a third country, to the extent the output produced by those systems is intended to be used in the Union. Nonetheless, to take into account existing arrangements and special needs for future cooperation with foreign partners with whom information and evidence is exchanged, this Regulation should not apply to public authorities of a third country and international organisations when acting in the framework of cooperation or international agreements concluded at Union or national level for law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or the Member States, provided that the relevant third country or international organisation provides adequate safeguards with respect to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. Where relevant, this may cover activities of entities entrusted by the third countries to carry out specific tasks in support of such law enforcement and judicial cooperation. Such framework for cooperation or agreements have been established bilaterally between Member States and third countries or between the European Union, Europol and other Union agencies and third countries and international organisations. The authorities competent for supervision of the law enforcement and judicial authorities under this Regulation should assess whether those frameworks for cooperation or international agreements include adequate safeguards with respect to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. Recipient national authorities and Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies making use of such outputs in the Union remain accountable to ensure their use complies with Union law. When those international agreements are revised or new ones are concluded in the future, the contracting parties should make utmost efforts to align those agreements with the requirements of this Regulation.
questions.examples:
- [Excluded] A public authority of a third country uses an AI system in the framework of a bilateral agreement with a Member State for law enforcement and judicial cooperation, provided that the agreement includes adequate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms. Source: Recital (22) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 29.
- [Excluded] An international organisation uses an AI system in the framework of cooperation or agreements for law enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union, for example agreements between the Union, Europol and other Union agencies and international organisations. Source: Recital (22) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Excluded where relevant] A private entity entrusted by the third country to carry out specific tasks in support of such law enforcement and judicial cooperation. Source: Recital (22) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 29.
- [Not excluded] A national authority or a Union institution, body, office or agency that makes use of such outputs in the Union remains accountable for ensuring that the use complies with Union law. Source: Recital (22) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 29.
- [Not excluded] The activities of Europol and other Union security agencies, such as Frontex, fall within the scope of the AI Act. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 28.

questions.question: Is the AI system used in research, testing or development activity and has not been placed on the market or put into service?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not apply to research, testing and development of AI systems or models before they are offered on the market or put into use. This also covers product-oriented, commercial work, such as a company developing its own AI product.

END OF THE EXCLUSION
The exclusion ends when the system is placed on the market or put into service. From that moment, the AI Act applies.

TESTING IN REAL-WORLD CONDITIONS
Testing in real-world conditions (outside the lab, with real users or real situations) is not excluded and is regulated by the AI Act.

OTHER APPLICABLE EU LAW
Even when the exclusion applies, the work must still comply with other EU law, such as data protection rules, research ethics rules and sector-specific rules.

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
RESEARCH, TESTING AND DEVELOPMENT BEFORE PLACING ON THE MARKET OR PUTTING INTO SERVICE

Summary:
Art. 2(8) excludes research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models before they are placed on the market or put into service; such activity must comply with applicable Union law, and testing in real world conditions is not covered by the exclusion. Art. 2(6) is the related exclusion for systems developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Recital 25 explains that the exclusion also covers product-oriented research, testing and development, ends once the system is placed on the market or put into service, and is without prejudice to regulatory sandboxes and real-world testing. Look here for: the boundary between pre-market development and market placement.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (8)  This Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion.

Art. 2 (6) This Regulation does not apply to AI systems or AI models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.

Art. 3(9) 'placing on the market' means the first making available of an AI system or a general-purpose AI model on the Union market;

Art. 3(11) 'putting into service' means the supply of an AI system for first use directly to the deployer or for own use in the Union for its intended purpose; 

Art. 3(57) 'testing in real-world conditions' means the temporary testing of an AI system for its intended purpose in real-world conditions outside a laboratory or otherwise simulated environment (...)

Recitals:
Recital (25): This Regulation should support innovation, should respect freedom of science, and should not undermine research and development activity. It is therefore necessary to exclude from its scope AI systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Moreover, it is necessary to ensure that this Regulation does not otherwise affect scientific research and development activity on AI systems or models prior to being placed on the market or put into service. As regards product-oriented research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models, the provisions of this Regulation should also not apply prior to those systems and models being put into service or placed on the market. That exclusion is without prejudice to the obligation to comply with this Regulation where an AI system falling into the scope of this Regulation is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity and to the application of provisions on AI regulatory sandboxes and testing in real world conditions. Furthermore, without prejudice to the exclusion of AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, any other AI system that may be used for the conduct of any research and development activity should remain subject to the provisions of this Regulation. In any event, any research and development activity should be carried out in accordance with recognised ethical and professional standards for scientific research and should be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law.

Guidelines
Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), C(2025) 5052 final (https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/112367):

(32) The exclusion in Article 2(8) AI Act is, however, without prejudice to the obligation to comply with the AI Act where an AI system is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity. (...) Testing in real-world conditions within the meaning of the AI Act (...) is also not covered by that exclusion.
questions.examples:
- [Not covered] During the research and development phase, AI developers experiment with and test new functionalities, including techniques that could be seen as manipulative if used in consumer-facing applications. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 30.
- [Not covered] Product-oriented research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models before they are put into service or placed on the market. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not covered] A general-purpose AI model used before its placing on the market for the sole purpose of research, development and prototyping activities. Source: Recital (97) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Covered] A municipality tests facial recognition software using a remote biometric identification system in the streets during carnival and recruits volunteers to be identified: testing in real-world conditions is not covered by the exclusion. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 32.
- [Covered] An AI system that is placed on the market or put into service as a result of research and development activity. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 32.
- [Covered] A public authority develops a scoring system in-house and deploys it to predict the risk of fraud of household allowance beneficiaries: this is putting into service for own use. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 13.

questions.question: Does a natural person use the system exclusively in the course of a personal, non-professional activity?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not impose obligations on individuals who use AI systems only for purely private purposes, for example at home, for hobbies or in family life. Such use is considered lower risk than professional or business use.

WHEN THE EXCLUSION DOES NOT APPLY
The exclusion does not apply when the system is used:
- for work, business or other professional activity,
- in an organised social or non-profit activity, for example in an association or foundation,
- for both private and professional purposes (mixed use).

INCOME FROM THE ACTIVITY
Earning some income does not automatically exclude private use, as long as the activity is not carried out professionally, as a business or as another organised activity.

SCOPE OF THE EXCLUSION AND CIVIL LIABILITY
This exclusion concerns only the private user. It does not release the provider of the system from its obligations. The private user may still be liable under civil law for damage caused intentionally or through gross negligence.

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
PURELY PERSONAL, NON-PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITY (EXCEPTION IV)

Summary:
Art. 2(10) states that the Regulation does not apply to the obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity. Recital 109 concerns general-purpose AI models: compliance obligations should be proportionate, persons who develop or use models for non-professional or scientific research purposes need not comply but are encouraged to do so voluntarily, and obligations in case of modification or fine-tuning are limited to that modification. Look here for: the wording "purely personal non-professional activity" (Art. 2(10)) and the treatment of non-professional use of general-purpose AI models (Recital 109).

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (10)  This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity.

Recitals:
Recital (109): Compliance with the obligations applicable to the providers of general-purpose AI models should be commensurate and proportionate to the type of model provider, excluding the need for compliance for persons who develop or use models for non-professional or scientific research purposes, who should nevertheless be encouraged to voluntarily comply with these requirements. Without prejudice to Union copyright law, compliance with those obligations should take due account of the size of the provider and allow simplified ways of compliance for SMEs, including start-ups, that should not represent an excessive cost and not discourage the use of such models. In the case of a modification or fine-tuning of a model, the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models should be limited to that modification or fine-tuning, for example by complementing the already existing technical documentation with information on the modifications, including new training data sources, as a means to comply with the value chain obligations provided in this Regulation.

Guidelines
Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), C(2025) 5052 final (https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/112367):

(34) Any activity through which a natural person gains an economic benefit on a regular basis or is otherwise involved in a professional, business, trade, occupational or freelance activity should be considered as a 'professional' activity. The specification of 'personal' is a qualifier of non-professional, meaning that the person should act in both a personal and a non-professional capacity. The exclusion should therefore, for example, not encompass criminal activities since these should not be considered purely personal. (...) Any use by natural persons where they are acting on behalf or under the authority of a deployer acting in a professional capacity will also fall within the scope of the AI Act. (...) Furthermore, criminal activities cannot be considered purely personal activities, even if no economic benefit is sought or attained (...)

(35) The exclusion in Article 2(10) AI Act applies only as regards the obligations of deployers when using the system for purely personal non-professional activities.
questions.examples:
- [Excluded] An individual uses a facial recognition system at home, for example to control access to the entrance of the home and to monitor it for safety, even where parts of the footage must be transmitted to law enforcement authorities. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 34.
- [Not excluded] A natural person uses an AI system for professional activities, for example as a freelancer, journalist or doctor. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 34.
- [Not excluded] A natural person uses an AI system on behalf or under the authority of a deployer acting in a professional capacity. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 34.
- [Not excluded] Criminal activities: they cannot be considered purely personal activities, even if no economic benefit is sought or attained. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 34.
- [Deployer excluded, system still covered] An emotion recognition system intended to be used by natural persons for purely personal non-professional activities (for example by an autistic person): the use is out of scope for the deployer, but the system remains a high-risk AI system for the provider. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 35.

questions.question: Is the system made available under a free and open-source licence?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE AND CONDITIONS
The AI Act generally does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences. To benefit from this exclusion, the system must meet all of the following conditions:
- Publicly available: anyone can access it on equal terms. Only basic steps, such as accepting terms of use, downloading the system or creating a user account, are acceptable.
- Free: there is no monetisation. Monetisation includes charging a price, charging for technical support or related services (also through software platforms), or using personal data for purposes other than improving security, compatibility or interoperability. Sharing the system in an open repository is not monetisation. Transactions between micro-enterprises are also not treated as monetisation.
- Open: key technical information, such as model weights, architecture and information on use, is publicly available, and the licence allows users not only to use, but also to modify and distribute the system.

LIMITS OF THE EXCLUSION
The exclusion does not apply if the system is placed on the market or put into service as a high-risk AI system, as a prohibited AI practice, or as a system subject to transparency obligations (for example, a system that generates or manipulates images, sound or video, such as deepfakes).

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
EXCLUSION FOR FREE AND OPEN-SOURCE LICENCES AND ITS LIMITS

Summary:
Art. 2(12) excludes AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as AI systems falling under Art. 5 (prohibited practices) or Art. 50 (transparency obligations). Recital 89 adds that third parties making tools, services, processes or AI components (other than general-purpose AI models) publicly accessible under a free and open-source licence should not be required to comply with value-chain responsibility requirements, while being encouraged to use documentation practices such as model cards and data sheets. Look here for: the three cases in which the exclusion does not apply (high-risk, Art. 5, Art. 50).

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (12)  This Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50.

Recitals:
Recital (89): Third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes, or AI components other than general-purpose AI models, should not be mandated to comply with requirements targeting the responsibilities along the AI value chain, in particular towards the provider that has used or integrated them, when those tools, services, processes, or AI components are made accessible under a free and open-source licence. Developers of free and open-source tools, services, processes, or AI components other than general-purpose AI models should be encouraged to implement widely adopted documentation practices, such as model cards and data sheets, as a way to accelerate information sharing along the AI value chain, allowing the promotion of trustworthy AI systems in the Union.


MEANING OF "FREE AND OPEN-SOURCE" AND MONETISATION

Summary:
Recital 102 describes licences that are to be considered free and open-source (users can run, copy, distribute, study, change and improve software and data, including models, subject to crediting the original provider and comparable distribution terms) and the transparency and openness of general-purpose AI models (public availability of weights, architecture and usage information). Recital 103 explains what counts as monetisation (a price, paid technical support or related services, use of personal data other than for security, compatibility or interoperability, with an exception for transactions between microenterprises) and that making components available in open repositories is not monetisation in itself. Look here for: the criteria of "free" and "open" and the monetisation test.

Recitals:
Recital (102): Software and data, including models, released under a free and open-source licence that allows them to be openly shared and where users can freely access, use, modify and redistribute them or modified versions thereof, can contribute to research and innovation in the market and can provide significant growth opportunities for the Union economy. General-purpose AI models released under free and open-source licences should be considered to ensure high levels of transparency and openness if their parameters, including the weights, the information on the model architecture, and the information on model usage are made publicly available. The licence should be considered to be free and open-source also when it allows users to run, copy, distribute, study, change and improve software and data, including models under the condition that the original provider of the model is credited, the identical or comparable terms of distribution are respected.

Recital (103): Free and open-source AI components covers the software and data, including models and general-purpose AI models, tools, services or processes of an AI system. Free and open-source AI components can be provided through different channels, including their development on open repositories. For the purposes of this Regulation, AI components that are provided against a price or otherwise monetised, including through the provision of technical support or other services, including through a software platform, related to the AI component, or the use of personal data for reasons other than exclusively for improving the security, compatibility or interoperability of the software, with the exception of transactions between microenterprises, should not benefit from the exceptions provided to free and open-source AI components. The fact of making AI components available through open repositories should not, in itself, constitute a monetisation.

Guidelines
Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), C(2025) 5052 final (https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/112367):

(36) (...) AI Act does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences (...) This means that providers of AI systems cannot benefit from this exclusion if the AI system they place on the market or put into service constitutes a prohibited practice under Articles 5 AI Act.

Commission Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), C(2026) 7702 final of 5 November 2026 (https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/131215):

(23) According to Article 2(12) AI Act, AI systems released under free and open-source licences are outside the scope of the AI Act provided they do not fall under the prohibitions of Article 5 AI Act or the transparency obligations of Article 50 AI Act, or they are not classified as high-risk (...)

(24) By contrast, providers of free and open-source AI components that cover software, data, models, tools, services or processes for customisation and integration into an AI system and that do not constitute in themselves (in part or in whole) an AI system, are not subject to the transparency obligations in Article 50 AI Act.
questions.examples:
- [Free and open-source] Software and data, including models, released under a licence that allows them to be openly shared and where users can freely access, use, modify and redistribute them or modified versions thereof. Source: Recital (102) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Free and open-source] A licence that allows users to run, copy, distribute, study, change and improve software and data, including models, under the condition that the original provider is credited and identical or comparable terms of distribution are respected. Source: Recital (102) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not free and open-source] A licence limited to non-commercial or research-only use, a licence that prohibits distributing the model, or a licence that requires additional licensing once the number of monthly active users exceeds a certain number (examples given for general-purpose AI models). Source: Commission Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, C(2025) 7719 final, para 80.
- [Monetisation, so no exclusion] A dual licensing model that allows free academic use but requires payment for commercial usage or use over a certain scale; users must purchase support, training and maintenance services to access the model; the model is exclusively hosted on the provider's platform, which requires payment for access or serves paid advertisements (examples given for general-purpose AI models). Source: Recital (103) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, C(2025) 7719 final, para 83.
- [Monetisation, so no exclusion] Access, use, modification or redistribution requires the collection or other processing of personal data, unless that processing is exclusively and strictly limited to the security of the model and without any commercial or financial gain. Source: Recital (103) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, C(2025) 7719 final, para 84.
- [Not monetisation] Purely optional paid services or support offered alongside the model, for example premium versions with advanced features, update systems, extensions or plug-ins; and transactions between microenterprises. Source: Recital (103) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on the scope of the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, C(2025) 7719 final, paras 85 and 86.
- [Exclusion does not apply] An AI system released under a free and open-source licence that is placed on the market or put into service as a high-risk AI system, as a prohibited practice under Article 5 or as an AI system under Article 50. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 36.

questions.question: Is the AI System's output used in the EU?
questions.ownerContext:
MILITARY, DEFENCE AND NATIONAL SECURITY
The AI Act does not cover an AI system that is used only for military, defence or national security purposes. It does not matter who uses it: a public body and a private company are treated alike. If the same system is also used for any other purpose, for example civilian, humanitarian or law enforcement, even occasionally, the exclusion is lost.

SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
The AI Act also does not cover AI systems that are developed and used only for scientific research and development. This includes research in all fields, not only technical sciences, but also the humanities and social sciences.

KEY CONDITION: "EXCLUSIVELY"
The key word is "exclusively". If the system is also used for any other purpose (for example civilian, commercial or law enforcement), the AI Act applies. The same is true if a system first built for military use is later used, even temporarily, for civilian or humanitarian purposes.

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
MILITARY, DEFENCE AND NATIONAL SECURITY (EXCEPTION IA)

Summary:
Art. 2(3) contains three separate rules: (1) areas outside the scope of Union law and the Member States' national security competences, (2) AI systems used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, (3) AI systems not placed on the market or put into service in the Union whose output is used in the Union exclusively for those purposes. Recital 24 explains the rationale (Art. 4(2) TEU) and the consequences of mixed use or a later change of purpose. Look here for: the "exclusively" test, the wording "regardless of the type of entity", and what happens when a system is also used for civilian, law enforcement or public security purposes.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (3).  This Regulation does not apply to areas outside the scope of Union law, and shall not, in any event, affect the competences of the Member States concerning national security, regardless of the type of entity entrusted by the Member States with carrying out tasks in relation to those competences.

This Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.

This Regulation does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union, where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.

Recitals:
Recital (24): If, and insofar as, AI systems are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification of such systems for military, defence or national security purposes, those should be excluded from the scope of this Regulation regardless of which type of entity is carrying out those activities, such as whether it is a public or private entity. As regards military and defence purposes, such exclusion is justified both by Article 4(2) TEU and by the specificities of the Member States’ and the common Union defence policy covered by Chapter 2 of Title V TEU that are subject to public international law, which is therefore the more appropriate legal framework for the regulation of AI systems in the context of the use of lethal force and other AI systems in the context of military and defence activities. As regards national security purposes, the exclusion is justified both by the fact that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States in accordance with Article 4(2) TEU and by the specific nature and operational needs of national security activities and specific national rules applicable to those activities. Nonetheless, if an AI system developed, placed on the market, put into service or used for military, defence or national security purposes is used outside those temporarily or permanently for other purposes, for example, civilian or humanitarian purposes, law enforcement or public security purposes, such a system would fall within the scope of this Regulation. In that case, the entity using the AI system for other than military, defence or national security purposes should ensure the compliance of the AI system with this Regulation, unless the system is already compliant with this Regulation. AI systems placed on the market or put into service for an excluded purpose, namely military, defence or national security, and one or more non-excluded purposes, such as civilian purposes or law enforcement, fall within the scope of this Regulation and providers of those systems should ensure compliance with this Regulation. In those cases, the fact that an AI system may fall within the scope of this Regulation should not affect the possibility of entities carrying out national security, defence and military activities, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities, to use AI systems for national security, military and defence purposes, the use of which is excluded from the scope of this Regulation. An AI system placed on the market for civilian or law enforcement purposes which is used with or without modification for military, defence or national security purposes should not fall within the scope of this Regulation, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities.


SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT (EXCEPTION IB)

Summary:
Art. 2(6) excludes AI systems and models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Recital 25 explains the rationale and the limits of the exclusion (e.g. systems placed on the market as a result of research remain covered; other systems used for research remain subject to the Regulation). Recital 109 concerns general-purpose AI models and persons who develop or use models for non-professional or scientific research purposes. Look here for: the "sole purpose" wording and the ethical and Union-law conditions that apply to research and development.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (6). This Regulation does not apply to AI systems or AI models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.

Recitals:
Recital (25): This Regulation should support innovation, should respect freedom of science, and should not undermine research and development activity. It is therefore necessary to exclude from its scope AI systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Moreover, it is necessary to ensure that this Regulation does not otherwise affect scientific research and development activity on AI systems or models prior to being placed on the market or put into service. As regards product-oriented research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models, the provisions of this Regulation should also not apply prior to those systems and models being put into service or placed on the market. That exclusion is without prejudice to the obligation to comply with this Regulation where an AI system falling into the scope of this Regulation is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity and to the application of provisions on AI regulatory sandboxes and testing in real world conditions. Furthermore, without prejudice to the exclusion of AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, any other AI system that may be used for the conduct of any research and development activity should remain subject to the provisions of this Regulation. In any event, any research and development activity should be carried out in accordance with recognised ethical and professional standards for scientific research and should be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law.
questions.examples:
- [Not excluded] An AI system developed for military purposes that is used outside those purposes, temporarily or permanently, for law enforcement or public security purposes: it falls within the scope of the AI Act. Source: Recital (24) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not excluded] An AI system placed on the market or put into service for a military purpose and, at the same time, for a non-excluded purpose such as civilian purposes or law enforcement: it falls within the scope of the AI Act. Source: Recital (24) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Excluded] An AI system placed on the market for civilian or law enforcement purposes which is used, with or without modification, for military, defence or national security purposes. Source: Recital (24) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Excluded] An AI system specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not excluded] Any other AI system that is merely used for the conduct of research and development activity remains subject to the AI Act. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

questions.question: Will the AI system be placed on the market or put into service in the EU?
questions.ownerContext:
RULE
The AI Act does not apply to research, testing and development of AI systems or models before they are offered on the market or put into use. This also covers product-oriented, commercial work, such as a company developing its own AI product.

END OF THE EXCLUSION
The exclusion ends when the system is placed on the market or put into service. From that moment, the AI Act applies.

TESTING IN REAL-WORLD CONDITIONS
Testing in real-world conditions (outside the lab, with real users or real situations) is not excluded and is regulated by the AI Act.

OTHER APPLICABLE EU LAW
Even when the exclusion applies, the work must still comply with other EU law, such as data protection rules, research ethics rules and sector-specific rules.

REFERENCES
M. Jędrzejczak, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] AI Act. Akt w sprawie sztucznej inteligencji. Komentarz, ed. M. Jędrzejczak, Ł. Szoszkiewicz, J. Wydra, Wolters Kluwer Polska, Warsaw 2025
P. Van Eecke, B. Regenhardt, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
C. Wendehorst, commentary on Art. 2 [in:] KI-VO: Verordnung über Künstliche Intelligenz. Kommentar, ed. M. Martini, C. Wendehorst, C.H.Beck, Munich 2024
questions.coContext:
RESEARCH, TESTING AND DEVELOPMENT BEFORE PLACING ON THE MARKET OR PUTTING INTO SERVICE

Summary:
Art. 2(8) excludes research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models before they are placed on the market or put into service; such activity must comply with applicable Union law, and testing in real world conditions is not covered by the exclusion. Art. 2(6) is the related exclusion for systems developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Recital 25 explains that the exclusion also covers product-oriented research, testing and development, ends once the system is placed on the market or put into service, and is without prejudice to regulatory sandboxes and real-world testing. Look here for: the boundary between pre-market development and market placement.

AI Act provision:
Art. 2 (8)  This Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion.

Art. 2 (6) This Regulation does not apply to AI systems or AI models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.

Art. 3(9) 'placing on the market' means the first making available of an AI system or a general-purpose AI model on the Union market;

Art. 3(11) 'putting into service' means the supply of an AI system for first use directly to the deployer or for own use in the Union for its intended purpose; 

Art. 3(57) 'testing in real-world conditions' means the temporary testing of an AI system for its intended purpose in real-world conditions outside a laboratory or otherwise simulated environment (...)

Recitals:
Recital (25): This Regulation should support innovation, should respect freedom of science, and should not undermine research and development activity. It is therefore necessary to exclude from its scope AI systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Moreover, it is necessary to ensure that this Regulation does not otherwise affect scientific research and development activity on AI systems or models prior to being placed on the market or put into service. As regards product-oriented research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models, the provisions of this Regulation should also not apply prior to those systems and models being put into service or placed on the market. That exclusion is without prejudice to the obligation to comply with this Regulation where an AI system falling into the scope of this Regulation is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity and to the application of provisions on AI regulatory sandboxes and testing in real world conditions. Furthermore, without prejudice to the exclusion of AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development, any other AI system that may be used for the conduct of any research and development activity should remain subject to the provisions of this Regulation. In any event, any research and development activity should be carried out in accordance with recognised ethical and professional standards for scientific research and should be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law.

Guidelines
Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), C(2025) 5052 final (https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/112367):

(32) The exclusion in Article 2(8) AI Act is, however, without prejudice to the obligation to comply with the AI Act where an AI system is placed on the market or put into service as a result of such research and development activity. (...) Testing in real-world conditions within the meaning of the AI Act (...) is also not covered by that exclusion.
questions.examples:
- [Not covered] During the research and development phase, AI developers experiment with and test new functionalities, including techniques that could be seen as manipulative if used in consumer-facing applications. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 30.
- [Not covered] Product-oriented research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models before they are put into service or placed on the market. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Not covered] A general-purpose AI model used before its placing on the market for the sole purpose of research, development and prototyping activities. Source: Recital (97) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.
- [Covered] A municipality tests facial recognition software using a remote biometric identification system in the streets during carnival and recruits volunteers to be identified: testing in real-world conditions is not covered by the exclusion. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 32.
- [Covered] An AI system that is placed on the market or put into service as a result of research and development activity. Source: Recital (25) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 32.
- [Covered] A public authority develops a scoring system in-house and deploys it to predict the risk of fraud of household allowance beneficiaries: this is putting into service for own use. Source: Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices, C(2025) 5052 final, para 13.

questions.question: System type and components: What kind of AI or automated decision-making is involved (e.g. large language model, classical ML classifier, computer vision model, rules engine, scoring algorithm, or a combination)? What are the specific models or components used, including names, versions, and providers where applicable?
System position: Is the AI the product itself, a component embedded in a wider product, or an API consumed by third parties?
Architecture: What are the main components and their boundaries? Which parts are AI-driven and which are deterministic? What are the key runtime dependencies?

Data flows: What types of data does the system take as input, where does it come from, and does it include sensitive or regulated categories? Does the output directly trigger a downstream action, or does it require human approval before anything happens?
Affected population: Who or what does the system’s output affect: the end user, a third party, or a downstream automated system?
Oversight and auditability: Is a human in, on, or in command of the loop? Are inputs, outputs, and decisions logged, and if so, for how long and retrievable by whom?
Update cadence: How often are models or decision logic updated or retrained, and who controls that process?
Failure behaviour: What does the system do when it cannot produce a reliable output or encounters an error?
What is the current development stage (e.g. proof of concept, pilot, beta, production)?
What is the planned rollout timeline and target regions or user groups?
Has any deployment already occurred, and if so, at what scale?
What is the AI system intended to be used for and what use cases does this AI system have specifically within the organisation?
questions.ownerContext:
The ‘intended purpose’ means the use for which an AI system is intended by the provider, including the specific context and conditions of use, [as specified in the information supplied by the provider in the instructions for use, promotional or sales materials and statements, as well as in the technical documentation] (Art. 3(12) EU AI Act).

When describing the intended purpose, it should be clearly stated:

- which business or operational tasks the AI system is intended to perform or support,
- which outputs the system provides (e.g., classifications, recommendations, or predictions),
- for what purpose these outputs are used (e.g., process acceleration, quality improvement, or decision support).

All intended purposes must be listed completely.

If a system has multiple use cases or applications, all of them must be identified, as the intended purpose is a key factor in determining the AI system's risk classification.
questions.descriptionGuidance: If there are multiple purposes, please list them all clearly and specifically. A risk classification and role assessment must occur for every intended purpose.

questions.question: Which use cases are specifically excluded from usage?
What specific output is created by the system?
Who is user of the AI system?
How often is the AI system to be used?
What consequences can wrong, distorted, or delayed usage of the AI system have?
Does the system make a final decision with legal or similarly significant effect?
Can a person effectively check, override, or stop the output of the AI system?

Does the AI system use biometric categorisation systems that categorise individual persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation?
questions.ownerContext:
WHAT IS PROHIBITED
Art. 5(1)(g) prohibits biometric categorisation systems that categorise natural persons individually on the basis of their biometric data in order to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Such categorisation systems are prohibited under the EU AI Act.

KEY TERMS
"Biometric data" means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data (Art. 3(34)).
A "biometric categorisation system" assigns natural persons to specific categories on the basis of their biometric data (Art. 3(40)); the definition does not cover a feature that is purely ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons (for example, filters on online marketplaces that let customers preview a product on themselves; Recital (16).

INDIVIDUAL CATEGORISATION
The prohibition applies only where persons are categorised individually. Systems that categorise a whole group without looking at the individual, or that are aimed at broad groups, are outside the prohibition (Commission Guidelines; commentary).

EXCLUSIONS
The prohibition does not cover the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets (for example, to make training data representative of all demographic groups) or the categorisation of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. The commentary notes that the wording of this exclusion is not fully clear.

REFERENCES
E.J. Kindt, C. Jasserand, commentary on Art. 5 [in:] The EU Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act: A Commentary, ed. C.N. Pehlivan, N. Forgó, P. Valcke, Kluwer Law International, Alphen aan den Rijn 2024
